rv.q: She pulls it off with power and finesse.
Morisseau has written a comedy about Black women who are ready to burn down their institutions.

It makes sense then that “Confederates,” which opened on Sunday at the Pershing Square Signature Theater, feels like an elegant experiment, thoughtful and put-together but not quite realizing its full potential.
I believe Morisseau is one of our finest working playwrights.
What stands out about the script, beyond its gorgeously scored points, is Morriseau's refusal to shove period language down our throats.
Morisseau’s satisfyingly troubling play takes place in two sometimes overlapping periods: today, as dominated by political science professor Sandra, and in the 1860s.
It is a provocative and powerful closing to a play less concerned with the individual stories it tells and more focused on the stubborn, lasting narrative those stories evoke.

Her thought-provoking play – sometimes deadly earnest and sometimes surprisingly (but intentionally) hilarious under Stori Ayers’ accomplished direction – focuses on two strong-willed African-American women, born over 150 years apart, but both trying to attain their own version of “freedom.”
At this moment, however, it looks like two half-realized plays stuck together, sometimes effectively, sometimes awkwardly.
Handled with much less finesse is the easy symmetry of the past and the present stories presented here.
The characters in Confederates sometimes seem more like ideas than people.
Ultimately, though, “Confederates” works better theatrically than dramatically or thematically.
Dominique Morisseau’s Confederates, the second play of her Signature Theatre Residency 5, is a clever, but overly talky dissertation on race, power and family.
Regrettably, this has the collateral effect of undercutting the urgency of the drama.
Director Stori Ayers skillfully navigates 'Confederates' between the satirical and the serious, and the rewards are great.

cn.t: Morisseau's ambitious dual-timeline drama about Black women facing oppression earns praise for sharp dialogue and bold ideas, but critics find it overstuffed and uneven, with more themes than one play can comfortably contain.
